title: The Real Reason Japan Attacked Pearl Harbor
keyword: why japan attacked pearl harbor (~29k/mes, +49 %) + the reason japan attacked pearl harbor (~14k) + pearl harbor (~244k, +129 %). vidIQ 21-nov-2026

scenes.text: On the morning of December the seventh, 1941, more than three hundred and fifty Japanese planes appeared over a quiet American naval base in Hawaii.
scenes.prompt: A calm tropical harbor at sunrise with palm trees and grey American battleships lined up in the water, and a large swarm of small planes with red circle markings appearing in the sky from the left.

scenes.text: In less than two hours, eight battleships were damaged or sunk, almost two hundred aircraft were destroyed, and more than two thousand four hundred Americans were dead.
scenes.prompt: Grey battleships in a harbor with cartoon orange flames and thick grey smoke rising from several of them, small planes with red circle markings flying away in the distance. No people shown, no blood.

scenes.text: It looked like madness. Japan had just attacked a country with ten times its industrial power. So why did it do it? The real answer is not about Hawaii at all. It is about oil.
scenes.prompt: Stick (the reporter) standing next to a balance scale: on the left side a small Japanese flag with a few factory icons, on the right side a big American flag with many more factories, the scale tipped heavily to the right. A single oil barrel with a question mark floats above.

scenes.text: To understand why, we need to go back to 1868. Japan had spent centuries closed off from the world. Then, almost overnight, it decided to modernise.
scenes.prompt: Split image: on the left a traditional Japanese village with samurai stick figures and wooden houses, on the right the same place transformed with a train, a factory chimney and stick figures in Western suits. The year 1868 written in marker at the top.

scenes.text: In just a few decades it built railways, factories and a modern navy. But Japan had a big problem: the islands had almost no oil, little iron and not enough rubber.
scenes.prompt: Simple map of the Japanese islands drawn in red outline, with three empty dotted circles next to it labelled with icons: an oil barrel, an iron ingot and a rubber tire, each with a small sad face, showing they are missing.

scenes.text: Everything that powered a modern country had to be shipped in from abroad. And Japan's leaders came to believe that the only way to be safe was to control those resources themselves.
scenes.prompt: Cargo ships carrying oil barrels, iron and rubber sailing across a blue sea toward the Japanese islands, Japanese stick figure leaders in suits on the shore looking worried and pointing at a map.

scenes.text: In 1905, Japan shocked the world by defeating Russia, a great European empire. Victory made its generals confident, and hungry for more.
scenes.prompt: A small Japanese stick figure soldier in khaki standing proudly on top of a big fallen Russian bear drawn in simple marker, the year 1905 written at the top.

scenes.text: In 1931, the Japanese army seized Manchuria, a region of northern China full of coal and iron. Then in 1937, Japan launched a full war against China.
scenes.prompt: A simple map of East Asia: Japan in red, China in light yellow, the northeast region of China being colored red with arrows coming from Japan, the years 1931 and 1937 written in marker.

scenes.text: The war in China turned into a brutal and endless struggle. Instead of a quick win, Japan was stuck, and its war machine was burning through fuel every single day.
scenes.prompt: A Japanese tank drawn in simple marker stuck in deep mud, its fuel gauge pointing at empty, tired Japanese stick soldiers pushing it, vast hills of China in the background.

scenes.text: And here is the twist. Most of that fuel came from the United States. Around eighty percent of Japan's oil was American.
scenes.prompt: A large pie chart drawn in marker, eighty percent colored blue with a small American flag, twenty percent grey, next to it a long pipeline running from a blue United States to a red Japan.

scenes.text: The Americans were selling oil to a country that was using it to fight a war they opposed. That could not last.
scenes.prompt: An American stick figure in a blue suit handing a big oil barrel to a Japanese stick figure general, while behind them a small Chinese stick figure looks on sadly. The American looks uneasy.

scenes.text: In 1940, Japan joined Nazi Germany and fascist Italy in the Tripartite Pact, and moved troops into French Indochina. Washington answered by cutting off scrap iron and steel.
scenes.prompt: Three stick figure diplomats signing a document at a table, the year 1940 written above, and in the corner a blue padlock locking a pile of scrap iron and steel beams.

scenes.text: Then, in July 1941, Japanese troops pushed into southern Indochina. This time President Franklin Roosevelt went all the way.
scenes.prompt: Simple map of Southeast Asia with red arrows moving south into Indochina, and on the right a stern American president stick figure in glasses and a dark suit at a desk, lifting a pen.

scenes.text: The United States froze Japan's money in American banks and stopped selling it oil. Britain and the Dutch did the same. Overnight, Japan lost almost all of its oil imports.
scenes.prompt: A big oil pipeline drawn in marker with a giant blue valve being shut, a red stop sign on it, and on the other side a small red Japan with empty oil barrels falling over.

scenes.text: Japan had stored enough oil for about two years at most. After that, its navy would be stuck in port, its planes on the ground, and its army in China would grind to a halt.
scenes.prompt: A large hourglass filled with black oil instead of sand, running out, next to a row of Japanese warships and planes drawn in simple marker, all slowly fading as the oil drains.

scenes.text: Japan's leaders saw only two choices. They could give in to American demands and pull out of China. Or they could take the oil they needed by force.
scenes.prompt: A Japanese stick figure general standing at a fork in a road: the left path leads to a white flag and a map of China being handed back, the right path leads to oil fields and a red arrow pointing south.

scenes.text: The oil they wanted was in the Dutch East Indies, today's Indonesia, along with rubber in British Malaya. But between Japan and those islands sat the Philippines, an American colony.
scenes.prompt: Simple map of Southeast Asia and the western Pacific: Japan in red at the top, the Dutch East Indies islands at the bottom with oil derrick icons, Malaya with rubber tree icons, and the Philippines in the middle colored blue with a small American flag.

scenes.text: And behind the Philippines, waiting in Hawaii, was the American Pacific Fleet. A year earlier, Roosevelt had moved it from California to Pearl Harbor, as a warning to Japan.
scenes.prompt: A map of the Pacific Ocean with a blue arrow showing a fleet of small grey battleships moving from California to Hawaii, the Hawaiian islands circled, and Japan in red on the far left.

scenes.text: The man who planned the attack was Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto. He had studied in America and knew its strength better than most Japanese leaders.
scenes.prompt: A Japanese admiral stick figure in a white naval uniform and cap, standing thoughtfully next to a small sketch of Harvard-style buildings and American factories with smoke, a thinking bubble over his head.

scenes.text: His idea was a gamble. Destroy the American fleet in one surprise blow, and Japan would have six months, maybe a year, to grab the oil and build a defensive wall across the Pacific.
scenes.prompt: The Japanese admiral stick figure pointing at a big map of the Pacific with a red dashed line drawn like a wall around Japan's new territory, a calendar showing 6 months, and a broken blue ship icon in Hawaii.

scenes.text: Yamamoto hoped that, after such a shock, the Americans would not want a long and costly war, and would accept a deal.
scenes.prompt: A Japanese stick figure and an American stick figure sitting at a negotiation table, the Japanese one offering a peace document, the American one with crossed arms, a large question mark between them.

scenes.text: Meanwhile, diplomats were still talking in Washington. In late November, the Americans demanded that Japan leave China and Indochina completely. For Tokyo, that was unacceptable.
scenes.prompt: Two diplomats in suits at a table in Washington, one American and one Japanese, the American sliding a document across the table, the Japanese diplomat looking shocked, the Capitol dome drawn in the background window.

scenes.text: On November the twenty sixth, six Japanese aircraft carriers quietly left the northern islands of Japan. They sailed across the stormy North Pacific in total radio silence.
scenes.prompt: Six Japanese aircraft carriers with red circle markings sailing in a line across a dark grey stormy sea with big waves, a crossed-out radio icon floating above them.

scenes.text: Early on Sunday, December the seventh, the first wave of planes took off. At seven forty eight in the morning, the attack began. The signal was sent: Tora, Tora, Tora.
scenes.prompt: Japanese planes with red circle markings taking off from the deck of an aircraft carrier at dawn, an orange sunrise behind them, a clock showing 7:48.

scenes.text: Torpedo planes struck the battleships lined up along Battleship Row. A bomb hit the USS Arizona and set off its ammunition. The ship sank in minutes.
scenes.prompt: A grey battleship labeled ARIZONA in a harbor with large cartoon orange flames and a tall column of grey and black smoke rising, other battleships lined up next to it. No people shown.

scenes.text: A second wave followed. Airfields across the island were hit before most American planes could even take off.
scenes.prompt: An airfield with rows of small American planes on the ground, several of them with cartoon flames and smoke, Japanese planes flying overhead, palm trees on the edge. No people hurt.

scenes.text: But Japan missed its most important targets. The American aircraft carriers were out at sea that morning. And the huge fuel tanks and repair yards were left almost untouched.
scenes.prompt: Stick (the reporter) pointing at a split board: on the left an empty pier with a dotted outline of an aircraft carrier and a check mark, on the right large round fuel tanks and cranes intact, with a big red circle around them.

scenes.text: On the same day, Japan also struck the Philippines, Malaya, Hong Kong, Guam and Wake Island. Pearl Harbor was only one part of a giant plan to grab Southeast Asia.
scenes.prompt: Map of the western Pacific and Southeast Asia with many red arrows spreading out from Japan at the same time toward the Philippines, Malaya, Hong Kong, Guam and Wake Island, small explosion stars at each target.

scenes.text: And because of delays in decoding a long message, Japan's formal break with the United States was delivered almost an hour after the bombs started falling.
scenes.prompt: Japanese diplomat stick figures rushing with a very long paper message through an office door, a wall clock showing they are late, typewriters on the desks.

scenes.text: The next day, Roosevelt called it a date which will live in infamy. Congress declared war almost unanimously. Three days later, Germany declared war on the United States.
scenes.prompt: An American president stick figure in glasses speaking at a podium with microphones, a large crowd of stick figure congressmen standing and applauding, American flags behind them.

scenes.text: Overnight, a divided America became united, and its factories turned to war. In the years that followed, it built ships and planes faster than Japan could ever hope to match.
scenes.prompt: A huge American factory with many smoking chimneys producing a long line of new warships and planes on a conveyor belt, stick figure workers cheering, a small chart arrow going up.

scenes.text: Just six months later, at the Battle of Midway, American planes sank four of the Japanese carriers that had attacked Pearl Harbor. The gamble had failed.
scenes.prompt: Four Japanese aircraft carriers with red circle markings tilting and sinking into a blue sea with cartoon smoke, American planes with blue star markings flying above. The word MIDWAY and the year 1942 written in marker.

scenes.text: So the real reason Japan attacked Pearl Harbor was not hatred, and not even America itself. It was oil, and a bet that a single blow could buy enough time to win a war Japan could not afford to lose.
scenes.prompt: Stick (the reporter) standing next to a whiteboard showing a simple chain of drawn icons connected by arrows: an oil barrel, a padlock, an hourglass, and a battleship, ending with a big question mark.

scenes.text: Instead, it woke up the most powerful industrial nation on Earth. If you want more history on the map, subscribe to WarMap Stick.
scenes.prompt: Stick (the reporter) giving a thumbs up in front of a simple world map, the Pacific Ocean circled with a dashed line, a red subscribe button drawn in marker next to him.
